title: Eight Arrested in Ayodhya Ram Temple Donation Scam. Now the Supreme Court Is Being Asked to Step In.
excerpt: A PIL demands a CBI probe and forensic audit of the Ram Janmabhoomi Trust, the local bar association has refused to defend the accused, and NRI donors who sent crores are demanding answers.
body:
The grand Ram Mandir in Ayodhya — consecrated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in January 2024 and built on the back of donations from millions of devotees across India and the diaspora — is now at the centre of a widening financial scandal that has embarrassed the BJP, triggered intervention from the Supreme Court, and left NRI donors who contributed crores demanding accountability.

Eight men connected to the temple's donation-handling operations were arrested last week and detained for 14 days by an Ayodhya court on Monday. Police have recovered approximately ₹79.85 lakh ($85,000) in cash from the accused, who are charged under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita with criminal breach of trust, theft by a person entrusted with property, handling stolen property, and criminal conspiracy, along with provisions of the Prevention of Corruption Act.

## How the Scam Worked

The accused — Avinash Shukla, Anukalp Mishra, Lavkush Mishra, Manish Kumar Yadav, Karunesh Pandey, Ramashankar Mishra, Subhash Srivastava, and Ramashankar "Tinnu" Yadav — were embedded in the temple's cash-counting apparatus. Tinnu Yadav, a former driver of Trust general secretary Champat Rai, allegedly had access to donation box keys. Subhash Srivastava, a former bank employee, supervised the counting staff. Karunesh Pandey is accused of manipulating financial receipts.

Investigators suspect the alleged misappropriation took place over a sustained period through systematic manipulation of the donation collection process. The arrests followed the submission of a preliminary report by a Special Investigation Team (SIT) constituted by the Uttar Pradesh government on June 13 at the request of the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust itself.

## Courts Circle In

The case has now reached India's highest court. A Public Interest Litigation (PIL) has been filed in the Supreme Court seeking a forensic audit of the Trust's finances and a court-monitored CBI investigation. The petition, addressed to Chief Justice Surya Kant, argues that donations — including cash, gold, silver, jewellery, and digital contributions — constitute trust property requiring transparent fiduciary management. It demands the immediate preservation of all evidence: CCTV footage, cloud backups, QR code and UPI payment records, bank deposit slips, vault access registers, and inventory records.

A vacation bench of Justices MM Sundresh and Sheel Nagu declined urgent listing on June 29 but directed the petitioners to furnish copies to the Registry, signalling the matter will be taken up in due course.

Separately, a PIL in the Allahabad High Court's Lucknow Bench seeks a CBI probe and a comprehensive forensic audit by the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG). The petition cites "institutional denial" by the Trust's own spokesperson, who initially dismissed media reports as "mere rumours."

## A Bar Association Boycott

In a remarkable step, the Ayodhya Bar Association has passed a resolution refusing to defend any of the eight accused. Members who break the boycott face a ₹5 lakh penalty per accused they represent. Association Secretary Shailendra Jaiswal said their sentiments had been "deeply hurt" as Hindus and as residents of Ayodhya — though he clarified the resolution applies only to local bar members, leaving the accused free to seek counsel from outside.

The boycott adds a layer of local outrage to a case that is already politically charged. Opposition parties, including former Kerala Chief Minister Pinarayi Vijayan of the CPI(M), have demanded a Supreme Court-monitored investigation and called for the dissolution of the Trust entirely.

## The Diaspora Angle

The Ram Mandir's construction was funded overwhelmingly by public donations — a fundraising drive that reached deep into NRI communities in the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, the Middle East, and Australia. Hindu diaspora organizations ran high-profile campaigns, and individual NRIs contributed sums ranging from a few hundred dollars to lakhs of rupees. For many, it was an act of faith as much as philanthropy.

The embezzlement allegations strike directly at that trust. Indian American community leaders have privately expressed frustration that the same institution they championed now faces questions about basic financial controls. The PIL's demand for a digital forensic audit — covering UPI records, payment gateways, and online donation portals — speaks directly to the modern infrastructure through which diaspora contributions flowed.

Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath, a BJP leader who made the Ram Mandir a centrepiece of his political identity, has warned that those involved will "face the consequences." But with the matter now before the Supreme Court and the Allahabad High Court, the political establishment may find that the consequences extend beyond eight arrested men.

The temple receives an estimated ₹3-5 crore daily in donations from an average of 50,000-70,000 visitors. How much of that has been accounted for — and how much has not — is the question India's courts are now preparing to answer.

*Sources: Reuters, Bar and Bench, LiveLaw, IndiaVerve, Madhyamam Online*
